subject: Chemistry
title: Equilibrium
summary: Equilibrium is dynamic: forward and backward reactions both continue, at equal rates — so concentrations appear constant. Equilibrium is reached only in a closed system.
Every reaction has an equilibrium constant (Kc, Kp) that depends only on temperature. Large K ⇒ mostly products; comparing Q with K tells which way a reaction will move.
Le Chatelier: disturb an equilibrium (change concentration, pressure or temperature) and the system shifts to reduce the change. A catalyst only gets there faster; it doesn't change the equilibrium.
Ionic equilibrium: strong electrolytes ionise fully, weak ones partly. Weak acid/base ionisation is described by Ka/Kb, water by Kw. pH = −log[H⁺].

Three big applications: buffers (keeping pH steady — Henderson equation), salt hydrolysis (pH of salt solutions), and solubility product Ksp (how much a sparingly soluble salt dissolves and when a precipitate forms).

formulas.name: Law of chemical equilibrium
formulas.when: Writing K for any reversible reaction.
formulas.mistake: Pure solids and pure liquids (and the solvent in dilute solutions) don't appear in K.

formulas.name: Kp and Kc
formulas.formula: Kp = Kc (RT)^{Δn_g}   (R = 0.0821 L·atm/(K·mol), p in atm)
formulas.note: Δn_g = moles of gaseous products − reactants; Δn_g = 0 ⇒ Kp = Kc.

formulas.name: Manipulating K
formulas.formula: Reverse reaction: K' = 1/K.   Reaction × n: K' = Kⁿ.   Add two reactions: K = K₁ × K₂
formulas.when: K of a new reaction from given ones.

formulas.name: Reaction quotient
formulas.formula: Q (same expression, concentrations at any moment):  Q < K → forward,  Q > K → backward,  Q = K → equilibrium

formulas.name: Degree of dissociation (example PCl₅)
formulas.formula: PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂:   Kp = α² P / (1 − α²)
formulas.when: Gas dissociation problems; α = fraction dissociated.
formulas.note: Total moles = 1 + α (starting with 1 mol PCl₅).

formulas.name: ΔG and K
formulas.formula: ΔG° = −RT ln K;   ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q;   at equilibrium ΔG = 0

formulas.name: Temperature dependence (van 't Hoff)
formulas.note: Endothermic: T up → K up. Exothermic: T up → K down.

formulas.name: Le Chatelier — quick table
formulas.formula: Add reactant → forward.  Raise pressure → side with fewer gas moles.  Raise T → endothermic side.  Catalyst → no shift.  Inert gas (constant V) → no shift;  (constant p) → side with more moles
formulas.note: Only temperature changes K; everything else changes only the position.

formulas.name: Henry's law
formulas.formula: p = K_H x   (partial pressure of a gas ∝ its mole fraction in solution)
formulas.when: Gases dissolving in liquids (soda, scuba diving).
formulas.note: Gas solubility decreases as temperature rises.

formulas.name: Ionic product of water
formulas.note: Kw rises with temperature — hot water's neutral pH is below 7 (still neutral).

formulas.name: Weak acid (Ostwald dilution law)
formulas.formula: α = √(Ka/C);   [H⁺] = √(Ka C);   pH = ½(pKa − log C)
formulas.when: pH and α of a weak acid.

formulas.name: Weak base
formulas.when: pH of a weak base like NH₃.

formulas.name: Conjugate pair
formulas.when: Kb of an acid's conjugate base (or vice versa).
formulas.note: A strong acid's conjugate base is very weak.

formulas.name: Polyprotic acids
formulas.formula: H₂A: Ka₁ ≫ Ka₂;   pH set almost entirely by Ka₁;  [A²⁻] ≈ Ka₂
formulas.note: The second proton is harder to remove (from a negative ion).

formulas.name: Common ion effect
formulas.formula: Weak acid HA + its salt (A⁻, conc C'):  α ≈ Ka / C'
formulas.note: A common ion lowers the α of a weak electrolyte.

formulas.name: Salt hydrolysis
formulas.formula: SA + SB: pH = 7.   WA + SB (CH₃COONa): pH = 7 + ½pKa + ½log C.   SA + WB (NH₄Cl): pH = 7 − ½pKb − ½log C.   WA + WB: pH = 7 + ½(pKa − pKb)  (independent of C)

formulas.name: Buffer (Henderson–Hasselbalch)
formulas.formula: Acidic: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]).   Basic: pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base])

formulas.name: Solubility product
formulas.formula: AₓB_y: Ksp = (xs)^x (ys)^y.   AB: s²,  AB₂/A₂B: 4s³,  AB₃/A₃B: 27s⁴,  A₂B₃: 108s⁵
formulas.when: Relation between solubility s (mol/L) and Ksp.
formulas.mistake: Don't compare solubilities of different salt types by Ksp alone — calculate s.

formulas.name: Precipitation and common ion
formulas.formula: Ionic product Q_sp > Ksp ⇒ precipitate.   AB in C M common ion: s ≈ Ksp / C
formulas.when: Will a precipitate form; solubility with a common ion.
formulas.note: Use the new (diluted) concentrations after mixing.

examples.title: Equilibrium concentration
examples.problem: A + B ⇌ C + D, Kc = 4. Initially [A] = [B] = 1 M. [C] at equilibrium?

examples.title: pH of a weak acid
examples.problem: 0.1 M CH₃COOH, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. [H⁺], pH and % ionisation?

examples.title: pH of a buffer
examples.problem: 0.1 M CH₃COOH + 0.2 M CH₃COONa, pKa = 4.74. pH?

examples.title: Ksp and common ion
examples.problem: Ksp of AgCl = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. Solubility in water? In 0.1 M NaCl?
examples.solution: Water: s = √Ksp = 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ M. In 0.1 M Cl⁻: s = Ksp/0.1 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M — about 7500 times less (common ion effect).

examples.title: Ksp from solubility (AB₂)
examples.problem: Solubility of CaF₂ is 2 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L. Ksp?

examples.title: Very dilute strong acid
examples.solution: Include H⁺ from water: [H⁺] = x, [OH⁻] = x − 10⁻⁸, x(x − 10⁻⁸) = 10⁻¹⁴ ⇒ x ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ M ⇒ pH ≈ 6.98 — slightly acidic, below 7.

topics.title: Dynamic equilibrium
topics.explain: Water in a closed bottle: evaporation and condensation continue at equal rates ⇒ constant vapour pressure. Chemical equilibrium is similar — it can be reached from either side.

topics.title: Physical equilibria
topics.explain: Solid ⇌ liquid (ice–water at 0 °C, 1 atm), liquid ⇌ vapour (vapour pressure in a closed vessel), solid ⇌ vapour (camphor, iodine — sublimation), gas ⇌ solution (CO₂ in soda — Henry's law). In each, some property becomes constant, and it happens only at a fixed temperature.

topics.title: Meaning of K
topics.explain: K > 10³: reaction goes almost to completion. K < 10⁻³: very little forward reaction. In between: significant amounts of both. K changes only with temperature, not with concentration or catalyst. Units of K depend on Δn.

topics.title: Classic Le Chatelier examples
topics.explain: Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, exothermic): high pressure and removing NH₃ push it forward; low T gives more yield but is slow — hence ~700 K with an Fe catalyst. N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ (endothermic): heating deepens the brown colour.

topics.title: Strong vs weak electrolytes
topics.explain: Strong (NaCl, HCl, NaOH): nearly 100% ions in water. Weak (CH₃COOH, NH₃): only slightly ionised, the rest molecules. On dilution the α of a weak electrolyte increases (Ostwald).

topics.title: Three acid–base concepts
topics.explain: Arrhenius: gives H⁺ in water = acid, gives OH⁻ = base (aqueous only). Brønsted–Lowry: proton donor = acid, acceptor = base; conjugate pairs (HCl/Cl⁻, NH₄⁺/NH₃). Lewis: electron-pair acceptor = acid (BF₃, AlCl₃, H⁺, metal ions), donor = base (NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻).

topics.title: Trends in acid strength
topics.explain: Larger Ka (smaller pKa) = stronger acid. Down a group bonds weaken ⇒ HF < HCl < HBr < HI. Across a period electronegativity rises ⇒ acidity CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF.

topics.title: pH scale
topics.explain: pH 7 is neutral (25 °C), < 7 acidic, > 7 basic. A change of 1 pH unit = 10 times in [H⁺]. Mixing two strong acids: add moles and divide by total volume.

topics.title: How a buffer works
topics.explain: Acidic buffer (CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa): added H⁺ combines with CH₃COO⁻, added OH⁻ is neutralised by CH₃COOH. Basic buffer: NH₃ + NH₄Cl. Blood buffer H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ (pH ≈ 7.4).

topics.title: Logic of salt hydrolysis
topics.explain: The anion of a weak acid (CH₃COO⁻) takes H⁺ from water and leaves OH⁻ ⇒ basic. The cation of a weak base (NH₄⁺) gives H⁺ ⇒ acidic. Ions from strong acids/bases don't hydrolyse (NaCl is neutral).

topics.title: Uses of Ksp
topics.explain: A precipitate forms when Q_sp > Ksp. Selective precipitation: the one with smaller Ksp precipitates first. A common ion lowers solubility; ions that form complexes (AgCl + NH₃) raise it.

ratta: Kp = Kc(RT)^{Δn_g};  reverse 1/K;  ×n → Kⁿ;  add → multiply.
Q < K forward, Q > K backward.
Only T changes K; a catalyst doesn't.
Hydrolysis: WA+SB pH = 7 + ½pKa + ½logC;  SA+WB pH = 7 − ½pKb − ½logC;  WA+WB pH = 7 + ½(pKa − pKb).
Ksp: AB s²,  AB₂ 4s³,  AB₃ 27s⁴,  A₂B₃ 108s⁵.
pH of 10⁻⁸ M HCl ≈ 6.98 (add water's H⁺).
